segments.title: Sicily, Carthage and Roman rivals in the game's opening speech
segments.body: The introductory game speech presents war as a family undertaking driven by revenge for deaths at Carthaginian, Greek and Roman hands. Its ambitions include making Sicily Roman, crushing Carthage and eliminating the other Roman families. The fictional narrator wants dominion over the world and links these victories to deserving the gods' love and the right to rule Rome. This is the game's dramatic framing of conquest and rivalry; it does not explain the historical course of the conflicts it invokes.

evidence.note: The opening speech invokes the gods, deaths caused by Carthaginians, Greeks and Romans, and a family undertaking in pursuit of vengeance.

The game narrator names Roman possession of Sicily, the crushing of Carthage, the removal of other Roman families and personal world dominion as the conditions for divine approval and worthiness to rule Rome.

segments.summary: Rome: Total War's opening speech frames conquest of Sicily, destruction of Carthage and conflict with rival Roman families as a personal quest for revenge and power.

segments.title: Rome: Total War and the limits of naval combat
segments.body: The original Rome: Total War was a childhood favorite at a time when many other players were absorbed in Halo. Its mix of history and battles was the main attraction, and the presence of ships made naval warfare part of that appeal. The naval system had strict limits: players received ships and fought naval engagements but could not control the vessels in battle. The clip ends with anticipation for returning to the game.

evidence.note: The original game identified as Dr. Clarke's childhood favorite.
The transcript links the appeal to history, battles, ships and naval fights, while specifying that players could not control ships in battle.
The transcript closes the clip by anticipating the game positively.

segments.summary: The original Rome: Total War's history, battles and ships made it a childhood favourite, although its naval engagements offered no direct control of the vessels.
